facts.statement: The genus Brochuchus was named by Conrad and colleagues in 2013.
Brochuchus lived during the Early Miocene epoch.
Fossils of Brochuchus have been found in the Hiwegi Formation on Rusinga Island in Lake Victoria, Kenya.
facts.quote: known from the Early Miocene Hiwegi Formation of Rusinga Island in Lake Victoria, Kenya

facts.statement: Brochuchus is classified within the crocodile family Crocodylidae.
facts.quote: Brochuchus belongs to the family Crocodylidae, which includes all living crocodiles.

facts.statement: Brochuchus had a flat, relatively narrow skull and was larger than the dwarf crocodile but smaller than most other crocodiles.
facts.quote: Brochuchus is characterized by a flat and relatively narrow skull, and although it is larger than Osteolaemus it is smaller than most other crocodylids.

facts.statement: Brochuchus belongs to the subfamily Osteolaeminae within the family Crocodylidae.
facts.quote: Brochuchus and Osteolaemus are part of a clade within Crocodylidae called Osteolaeminae.

facts.statement: Brochuchus was likely a predatory animal that spent most of its time in water.
facts.quote: Like most other species within Crocodylidae, Brochuchus was probably predatory and likely spent much of its time in water.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Brochuchus may have preyed on the early ape Proconsul, though there is no direct fossil evidence of its diet.
facts.quote: Although there is no direct evidence for what Brochuchus ate, it may have preyed on Proconsul.

facts.statement: If it preyed on apes, Brochuchus could be one of the earliest known "ape-eating" crocodilians.
facts.quote: If this is the case, Brochuchus may have been one of the earliest anthropoidophagous ("ape-eating") crocodilians.

facts.statement: Brochuchus is placed in the subfamily Osteolaeminae.
Brochuchus lived between 20.45 and 13.82 million years ago, spanning the Burdigalian to Langhian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Burdigalian to Langhian (20.45 to 13.82 million years ago)

facts.statement: Brochuchus is described as the most generalist member of the Osteolaeminae clade with a long snout.
